title: Fire in the Ground
description: Centralia's mine fire, Turkmenistan's burning gas crater and Australia's Burning Mountain

concepts.title: Centralia: The Town Above the Fire
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1981, a 12-year-old named Todd Domboski noticed thin wisps of smoke curling out of a grassy patch near a tree by his house in Centralia, Pennsylvania. He went over to look, and the ground gave way beneath his feet. His teenage cousin, Eric Wolfgang, pulled him out of the hole in less than a minute.1 The smoke came from a fire that had been burning under the town for almost 20 years.

The Centralia mine fire has burned in the abandoned deep mine workings of the Buck Mountain coal bed since May 1962. The state's official account says it reportedly began as a deliberate burn of household trash in an old strip-mine pit, and that without a proper fireproof barrier of shale, the flames are believed to have spread into waste coal and then into the mines.2

A coal seam is a buried layer of fuel, and old mines riddle it with tunnels. The fire draws its air through those connected workings and through cracks in the rock and soil above, and it needs very little: a coal fire can smolder with as little as 1 to 2% oxygen.3 Hot gases find their own way up, so smoke and steam rise from cracks that are not always above the burning coal. Borehole readings in the 1970s and 1980s often topped 1,000°F, and the highest was about 1,350°F (roughly 730°C).4 As the coal burns away, the ground above loses its support and can collapse without warning.

A federal study in 1983 estimated that putting the fire out would cost $663 million, so the government moved the town instead. Congress set aside $42 million for voluntary buyouts, and between 1985 and 1991, 545 homes and businesses were bought and their residents moved. A borough of about 1,100 people in 1962 was down to five property owners by 2013.5

concepts.title: Darvaza: The Door to Hell
concepts.contentHtml:
In the desert of northern Turkmenistan there is a pit about 69 meters (225 feet) wide and 30 meters (99 feet) deep, and it is on fire. Its nickname is the Door to Hell. In November 2013 the explorer George Kourounis climbed down into it on ropes, in a heat-reflective suit and carrying his own air, to collect soil from the floor. He found bacteria living at the bottom that were very comfortable in the heat and were not found in the soil outside the crater.1

The fuel is natural gas, mostly methane, which seeps up through the crust across the gas-rich Amu Darya basin. The story most often told is that in 1971 a Soviet gas-drilling rig broke into an underground gas reservoir, the ground collapsed beneath it, and geologists set the crater alight, expecting the gas to burn off within a few weeks.2 The paper trail is thinner than the legend. Local Turkmen geologists told Kourounis that the collapse may have happened in the 1960s and that the crater went unlit until the 1980s, and he could find no records to settle it.3

Whatever the date, lighting it had a logic. Unburned gas could suffocate people in nearby villages, and burning turns methane into carbon dioxide, which does less harm to the climate than raw methane leaking into the air.4 Turkmenistan's president first called for the fire to be put out in 2010. In June 2025 the head researcher at the state gas company, Turkmengaz, said that reopened wells nearby were drawing gas away and that the fires had shrunk "nearly threefold". In December 2025 the company announced a new well meant to divert the gas and end the uncontrolled emissions. A gas engineer told RFE/RL that even then, some gas may still find its way into the crater.5

concepts.title: Burning Mountain: The Fire That Walks
concepts.contentHtml:
Early European settlers in New South Wales saw smoke rising from a hill near Wingen and at first took it for a volcano. It is not one. Beneath Mount Wingen, better known as Burning Mountain, a coal seam has been smoldering for thousands of years. Sulfurous smoke still seeps out through vents, and the heat from below has baked the soil red and withered the plants over about half a hectare.1

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service calls it Australia's only naturally burning coal seam.2 The fire front lies about 30 meters underground and is heading south, so the burning mountain actually moves, about 1 meter a year. As the fire eats the coal, the rocks above slip into the gap, cracking and slumping the surface. The park service estimates that it has been burning for as much as 5,500 years.3 At a meter a year, that is long enough to creep several kilometers.

The age is not settled. Live Science reported the fire as at least 5,500 years old and noted that some geologists suspect it could be as old as 500,000 years. Researchers suspect that lightning lit coal exposed at the surface, but nobody saw it happen. A University of Sydney fire ecologist told the magazine that, being that far down, it is really too hard to put out now.4

The Wanaruah people, whose traditional territory took in the mountain, tell it differently. In their story, a woman waiting for her husband to come home from battle asked the sky god Biami to take her life when he did not return. Biami turned her to stone instead, and her tears became fire and set the mountain alight for all eternity.5

title: Waters That Kill and Bleed
description: Lake Nyos's deadly gas cloud, Antarctica's Blood Falls and the Amazon's Boiling River

concepts.title: Lake Nyos: The Lake That Breathed Out
concepts.contentHtml:
On the evening of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos, a crater lake in the volcanic highlands of northwest Cameroon, let out a sudden, enormous burst of gas. Survivors woke 6 to 36 hours later; many found that their oil lamps had gone out while still holding oil. About 1,700 people and 3,000 cattle died near the lake and along valleys up to 10 kilometers to the north.1 A later scientific count puts the human toll at 1,746.2

The gas was carbon dioxide, and the lake had been storing it. Nyos fills a crater blasted out by a volcanic explosion, and it is 208 meters deep. Carbon dioxide from deep magma seeps into its bottom water. Most lakes mix from top to bottom now and then, letting dissolved gas escape, but Nyos is stratified: lighter water sits on top of denser water and the two barely mix. So the gas builds up below, held in solution by the pressure of the water above, like the fizz in an unopened soda bottle. When the release came, the gas rushed out of solution, rose, expanded and pushed the water above it upward. Pure CO2 is about 1.5 times as dense as air, so the cloud hugged the ground and spilled down the valleys, pushing out the air people needed to breathe. The U.S. scientific team found that no volcanic eruption was involved, and it could not determine what set the release off.3

Nyos kept recharging with gas, so scientists decided to let it out on purpose. Controlled degassing began in 2001, despite fears that disturbing the lake might trigger another burst; measurements later showed that the layering was holding.4 The method is a pipe from the deep water to the surface. A pump lifts the first water up the pipe; as it rises, its gas comes out, and the bubbling column keeps the flow going on its own. Two more pipes were added in 2011.5

concepts.title: Blood Falls: The Glacier That Bleeds
concepts.contentHtml:
At the snout of Taylor Glacier, in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica, a rust-red stain spills down a wall of white ice. The geologist Griffith Taylor came across it in 1911.1 It was named Blood Falls, and its color was at first put down to red algae.2

The real source is a pool of very salty water trapped under about 400 meters of ice for at least 1.5 million years, probably the remains of an old salt lake that the glacier advanced over. The brine comes out cold and clear. It is about two and a half times as salty as seawater, holds no dissolved oxygen and carries plenty of dissolved iron, which the grinding glacier scrapes from the bedrock. Microbes live in it without sunlight. They get their energy by moving electrons from the sulfate in the water to the iron.3

A puzzle remained: how does liquid water flow out of a glacier whose ice is far below freezing? In 2017 a team using radar traced a path of brine through the ice to the falls. Salt lowers the freezing point, and, as the glaciologist Erin Pettit explained, water releases heat as it freezes, and that heat warms the surrounding colder ice, which keeps the brine moving. That makes Taylor Glacier the coldest known glacier with persistently flowing water.4

Even the red is subtler than plain rust. The color appears when the dissolved iron meets the air. A 2022 study of the stain found no strong sign of ordinary crystalline iron-oxide minerals. Instead, the iron oxidizes into tiny iron-rich spheres of non-crystalline material, and those give Blood Falls its color.5

concepts.title: The Boiling River of the Amazon
concepts.contentHtml:
As a boy in Lima, Andrés Ruzo heard his grandfather tell a legend from the Spanish conquest of Peru: the few who came back from the Amazon told of poisoned arrows, snakes that swallowed men whole and a river that boiled. Years later, studying Peru's geothermal energy for a PhD at SMU, he asked colleagues whether such a river could exist. The answer was a unanimous no. Boiling rivers do exist, but they are generally found near volcanoes, and the Amazon has none.1

Then his aunt said she had swum in it. In 2011 she guided him into the jungle, more than 700 kilometers from the nearest volcanic center, to a river whose average temperature, when he measured it, was 86°C (187°F).2 At its hottest spots the water can reach 200°F (about 93°C). Its Indigenous name, Shanay-timpishka, means "boiled with the heat of the sun."3

What heats it? Ruzo's answer is fault-fed hot springs. The deeper you go into the Earth, the hotter it gets, a rise called the geothermal gradient. Water, possibly from as far away as glaciers in the Andes, seeps deep underground, heats up and comes back to the surface along cracks and faults, turning a cold stream hot for 6.24 kilometers. In 2014 he said his data showed the river is neither magmatic nor volcanic in origin, and that he knew of no other non-volcanic geothermal system of this size, though more research was needed. Above about 47°C the water starts to hurt, and Ruzo has seen many animals fall in and not get out.4

The heat spills into the forest too. University of Miami biologists used the river as a natural experiment for a warmer Amazon and found an 11 percent drop in tree diversity for each degree of warming.5

title: Nature's Own Machines
description: A two-billion-year-old nuclear reactor, Death Valley's sailing stones and dunes that sing

concepts.title: Oklo: The Reactor Nobody Built
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1972 a routine check at a French nuclear fuel plant turned up uranium that should not exist. Everywhere else, in Earth's crust, in Moon rocks and even in meteorites, uranium-235 (the isotope that can sustain a nuclear chain reaction) makes up 0.720% of natural uranium. Ore from the Oklo mine in Gabon had only 0.717%, and further tests found one part of the mine short by some 200 kilograms of it, enough for half a dozen nuclear bombs.1

The obvious suspicion was that the uranium had already been through a man-made reactor. It had not. The physicist Francis Perrin and his colleagues confirmed that the ore was entirely natural, yet it was laced with fission products, the lighter elements left behind when uranium atoms split. The rock had run a nuclear reactor by itself, some two billion years ago.2

Why then, and never since? Uranium-235 decays about six times faster than uranium-238, so the further back in time you go, the richer natural uranium was in it. Two billion years ago it made up about 3%, roughly the level in the enriched fuel of most nuclear power stations. Water seeping through the ore did the job of a reactor's moderator, slowing the neutrons so they could split more nuclei.3 Today uranium-235 has decayed too far for any deposit to repeat the trick.4

The reactors even regulated themselves. When the heat of fission boiled the water away, the chain reaction stalled; once the rock cooled and water seeped back, it started again. Xenon gas trapped in mineral grains records the rhythm: one reactor ran for about 30 minutes, then shut down for at least 2.5 hours, like a slow geyser. Sixteen reactor zones are known in Oklo and the neighboring Okelobondo mine, and they kept pulsing for hundreds of thousands of years without a single meltdown or explosion.5

concepts.title: The Stones That Sail Across Death Valley
concepts.contentHtml:
Racetrack Playa is a dry lakebed in Death Valley National Park, flat as a table. Scattered across it are hundreds of rocks that seem to have been dragged across the ground, some weighing as much as 320 kilograms (700 pounds), each at the end of a groove in the mud that can run for hundreds of meters.1 For decades nobody saw one move. Trails were reported from 1948 on, and the rocks were blamed on very strong winds, dust devils, slick films of algae and thick sheets of ice that floated them off the mud.2

In 2011 a team led by Richard Norris of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography put up a weather station and planted 15 rocks fitted with motion-triggered GPS units (the Park Service would not let them use native rocks, so they brought look-alikes). Because the stones can sit for a decade or more without budging, co-author Ralph Lorenz expected "the most boring experiment ever." Then, in December 2013, Norris and his cousin Jim arrived to find the playa under a pond about 7 centimeters (3 inches) deep, and the rocks started to move.3

The mover turned out to be ice, but not the thick sheets the old theories needed. On cold nights the pond froze into "windowpane" ice just 3 to 6 millimeters thick. In the late-morning sun it broke up with a chorus of popping, and light winds of about 4 to 5 meters per second drove floating panels tens of meters wide into the rocks, bulldozing them along at 2 to 5 meters a minute. On December 20, 2013, more than 60 rocks moved at once.4

That pace is easy to miss. "It's possible that tourists have actually seen this happening without realizing it," Jim Norris said. The right mix of water, ice and wind is so rare that, by Lorenz's estimate, the rocks move only about one millionth of the time.5

concepts.title: Dunes That Sing
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1835, in the Chilean valley of Copiapó, Charles Darwin heard townspeople describe a hill they called El Bramador, "the roarer or bellower." As far as he could make out, the hill was covered in sand, and it made its noise only when people climbing it set the sand moving.1

Darwin was not the first to hear of singing sand. Marco Polo described it some 700 years ago and put it down to evil spirits. More than 30 singing dunes are now known around the world, each with its own note. The sound starts when sand piled near the crest avalanches down the steep face; it can drone for several minutes, carry more than a kilometer and pass for a low-flying airplane. Why the grains hum in unison is fiercely disputed: two former colleagues in Paris fell out so badly over it that they could no longer work in the same institution.2

Stéphane Douady and colleagues compared singing dunes with experiments in the field and the laboratory, and concluded that some sliding grains fall into step, synchronized by a resonance inside the flowing layer.3 A Caltech team including Nathalie Vriend and Melany Hunt disagreed: their field measurements put the boom at about 70 to 105 hertz, set by the dune itself. In their model a surface layer of dry, loose sand, sandwiched between regions where sound travels faster, acts as a waveguide whose depth fixes the pitch.4 Bruno Andreotti, Douady's former student turned rival, rejects resonance altogether. His group argues that the Caltech data show no link between the booming frequency and the predicted resonance.5

Everyone agrees that moving grains make the sound. What tunes them is still an open question.

title: Shapes That Fool the Eye
description: The Giant's Causeway, the Sahara's Eye that is no crater, and Tutankhamun's desert-glass scarab

concepts.title: The Giant's Causeway: Built by Cooling
concepts.contentHtml:
At the foot of the cliffs on Northern Ireland's north coast, some 40,000 black basalt columns step down into the sea, their flat tops forming a pavement of polygons. The sight has inspired legends of giants striding over the sea to Scotland.1 In one popular version, the Irish giant Finn McCool built the causeway to fight his Scottish rival Benandonner, then took fright. His wife Oonagh dressed him as a baby, and when Benandonner saw the size of the "infant," he decided he had no wish to meet the father and fled home, ripping up the causeway behind him.2

The real builder was lava. About 60 million years ago, as the ancient continent of Laurasia began to break apart and the North Atlantic opened, eruptions flooded the region. At the Causeway, lava drained into a valley and pooled as a lake some 90 meters deep. It cooled slowly and evenly, and as it cooled it shrank, opening contraction cracks that ran through the whole mass and split it into thousands of columns. The same eruptions built the columns of Staffa, an island off the west coast of Scotland.3 There, waves have hollowed the basalt into Fingal's Cave, whose acoustics inspired Mendelssohn's Hebrides Overture.4

Why columns, and why polygons? Cooling lava shrinks unevenly: the cooler part contracts against the hotter rock beside it until the stress cracks it. In a thick flow, a cooling front creeps inward and a crack front follows just behind, and as it advances the crack network orders itself into a roughly hexagonal pattern. Each jerk forward leaves a chisel-like band, a stria, on the column faces. Slow cooling makes wide columns, and fast cooling narrow ones. Physicists grow the same pattern in drying cornstarch, where losing water does what losing heat does to lava; the starch columns are just millimeters across.5

concepts.title: The Eye of the Sahara
concepts.contentHtml:
Seen from orbit, the Sahara has a bullseye. On the Adrar Plateau of Mauritania, concentric rings of rock 40 kilometers (25 miles) across circle a common center. French geographers described it in the 1930s, and photographs taken by the Gemini IV astronauts Ed White and James McDivitt made it famous as the Eye of the Sahara. Because large meteorites can blast circular scars, it was first thought to be an impact crater.1

The suspicion was reasonable, since three genuine impact craters were found in the same desert in 1952. But in 1969 the American geologist Robert Fudali showed the Richat could not be one, and a 2005 study confirmed that it is an eroded dome, formed when molten rock pushed up from beneath. The rock layers bulged upward like a blister; wind and sand then planed off the top and carved the bulge into circular ridges, leaving the oldest rocks in the middle and the youngest at the edges. It is so wide that a person standing inside it would have no idea they were in a circle.2

The full story took two acts. A 2024 study suggests that two sheets of gabbro, a dark igneous rock, were injected between the sedimentary layers probably 230 to 200 million years ago, during a vast volcanic episode known as the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province. Roughly 100 million years later a second, alkaline intrusion pushed the whole stack up into a dome 40 kilometers wide, and erosion has since flattened it into rings.3

Online, the rings are often offered as the ruins of Atlantis, the island civilization Plato described in his dialogues around 360 BCE. Geologists answer that the structure predates humans by tens of millions of years.4 Plato's own account does not fit either: his Atlantis was an island that, in one grievous day and night, "was swallowed up by the sea and vanished."5

concepts.title: Tutankhamun's Scarab of Desert Glass
concepts.contentHtml:
Among the treasures Howard Carter found in Tutankhamun's tomb, discovered in 1922, is a pectoral (a chest ornament) with a translucent, greenish-yellow scarab beetle at its center. It was long taken for chalcedony, a common form of quartz. Only in 1998 was it recognized as natural glass from the Libyan Desert Glass area, in the Great Sand Sea of Egypt's Western Desert some 800 kilometers west of the Nile. No other object made of this glass is known from the Nile Valley.1

The glass formed about 29 million years ago, when quartz sand melted at more than 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit (about 1,650°C), hotter than the inside of a volcano. Researchers have long argued over two answers: a meteorite striking the ground, or an airburst, a space rock exploding in the sky before it lands.2

The airburst idea had a strong point in its favor. The glass is spread over about 6,500 square kilometers, its chemistry suggests an impact, and yet no crater has been found. In 2006 Mark Boslough of Sandia National Laboratories simulated a 120-meter asteroid exploding low over the desert with the energy of more than 100 megatons. Its fireball, hotter than the melting point of quartz, touched the ground across an area 10 kilometers wide for more than 10 seconds: enough, in principle, to melt sand without digging a crater.3

In 2019 Aaron Cavosie and Christian Koeberl tested the idea inside the glass itself. Some tiny zircon crystals in it had once been reidite, a high-pressure mineral that forms only in the shock of a meteorite impact. Airbursts can melt the ground but cannot make such minerals, so the glass points to an impact, not a 100-megaton airburst.4 The crater is still missing. It may lie beneath shifting dunes, or have worn away until it can no longer be picked out on the landscape.5
